stem: A liver transplant candidate with hepatopulmonary syndrome (HPS) asks why transplantation is recommended. Which counseling point aligns with standard references?

options.text: Liver transplantation is the only available treatment option for HPS
HPS permanently excludes liver transplantation in every candidate
HPS resolves spontaneously without transplantation in most candidates
Isolated kidney transplantation is the primary treatment for HPS

explanation.rationale_correct: Hepatopulmonary syndrome is associated with increased mortality, and liver transplant is the only available treatment option.

rationale_incorrect.B: HPS and hepatorenal syndrome are reversible with transplantation and are not contraindications to liver transplantation.
rationale_incorrect.C: HPS is a complication of chronic liver failure that requires transplant rather than expected spontaneous resolution.
rationale_incorrect.D: HPS is a pulmonary complication of liver failure addressed through liver rather than isolated kidney transplantation.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 1, Evaluation → Liver transplantation → Additional evaluation → 4.b.i.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: HPS is associated with increased mortality and liver transplant is the only available treatment option

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 1 → Liver transplantation → Additional evaluation → 4.b.i. (HPS mortality; liver transplant as only treatment); PDF p. 44 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. First hepatopulmonary-syndrome item in bank; distinct from liver alcohol abstinence (cctc-1058) and smoking contraindication (cctc-1034); anchor verified on Cupples p. 44.

stem: A coordinator is updating cytomegalovirus (CMV) long-term complication teaching. Evaluate the following statements about organ-specific CMV effects on allografts:

elements.text: CMV may contribute to vanishing bile duct syndrome in liver allografts.
CMV may contribute to coronary artery vasculopathy in heart allografts.
CMV may contribute to bronchiolitis obliterans in lung allografts.
CMV may contribute to glomerulopathy in kidney allografts.

explanation.rationale_correct: Standard references list organ-specific CMV effects on allografts as vanishing bile duct syndrome in liver, coronary artery vasculopathy in heart, bronchiolitis obliterans in lung, and glomerulopathy in kidney.

rationale_incorrect.A: Statements III and IV are also correct—lung bronchiolitis obliterans and kidney glomerulopathy are listed organ-specific CMV effects.
rationale_incorrect.B: Statement IV is also correct—kidney glomerulopathy is a listed CMV organ-specific effect.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statements I and II are also correct—liver and heart organ-specific CMV effects are listed.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → CMV → 8. Organ-specific effects on allograft
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Liver: vanishing bile duct syndrome … Heart: coronary artery vasculopathy … Lung: bronchiolitis obliterans … Kidney: glomerulopathy

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 5 → CMV → 8. Organ-specific effects on allograft (liver, heart, lung, kidney); PDF p. 202 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Synthesized item. Eighteenth complex_combo in bank; CMV organ-specific angle distinct from CMV prevention strategies (cctc-1069) and toxoplasmosis combo (cctc-1064); anchor verified on Cupples p. 202.

stem: When counseling a potential living liver donor about surgical risk compared with living kidney donation, which teaching point aligns with standard living donor references?

options.text: Liver donation carries higher risk than kidney donation but is considered safe enough at experienced centers
Living liver donation has no surgical risk when performed at any hospital
Living kidney donation carries higher perioperative risk than living liver donation
Living liver donation is prohibited in all transplant programs

explanation.rationale_correct: Medical outcomes show that although liver donation portends a higher risk than kidney donation, it is still believed to be safe enough to perform at experienced centers.

rationale_incorrect.B: Liver donation carries higher risk than kidney donation and requires experienced center expertise.
rationale_incorrect.C: Kidney donation is described as safe with minimal ESRD risk; liver donation carries higher risk than kidney donation.
rationale_incorrect.D: Living liver donation is performed at experienced centers rather than being universally prohibited.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 7, Care of Living Donors → Introduction → 5.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: liver donation portends a higher risk than kidney donation, it is still believed to be safe enough to perform at experienced centers

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 7 → Introduction → 5. (liver donation higher risk than kidney; safe at experienced centers); PDF p. 331 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Living-liver surgical-risk comparison distinct from living-kidney ESRD counseling (cctc-1039) and liver donor discharge teaching (cctc-1061); anchor verified on Cupples p. 331.

stem: When explaining pretransplant infectious-disease screening to a solid-organ candidate, why is Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) status assessed?

options.text: EBV is associated with posttransplant lymphoproliferative disease that can affect graft and patient survival
EBV screening determines ABO compatibility before transplantation
EBV status has no relationship to post-transplant malignancy risk
EBV screening replaces the need for any cytomegalovirus prophylaxis planning

explanation.rationale_correct: EBV is associated with immunosuppression-related lymphoproliferative disease; posttransplant lymphoproliferative disease can affect both graft and patient survival, and EBV status is established by IgG antibody testing.

rationale_incorrect.B: EBV serology guides PTLD risk and prophylaxis planning rather than ABO compatibility.
rationale_incorrect.C: EBV is classified as a carcinogen associated with lymphoproliferative disease after transplantation.
rationale_incorrect.D: EBV and CMV screening serve different prophylaxis roles rather than replacing one another.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 1, Evaluation → Infectious disease screening → v. Epstein-Barr virus
primary_anchor.quote_hint: immunosuppression-related lymphoproliferative disease … Posttransplant lymphoproliferative disease can affect both graft and patient survival

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 1 → Infectious disease screening → v. Epstein-Barr virus (PTLD risk; graft and patient survival impact; IgG testing); PDF p. 29 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. EBV/PTLD screening angle distinct from CMV prevention combo (cctc-1069) and transplantation-risk combo (cctc-1054); anchor verified on Cupples p. 29.
